title: Knowledge Check 2: Lessons 6-10
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 6-10 of the ai-power-user series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: Ali wants her weekly delivery update to feed directly into the team's shared tracker so she stops re-typing rows by hand. Per the lesson, what is the step she should take in her prompt to make that handoff clean?
options: Ask for the work items as a JSON list with the exact field names (item, owner, status, blocker) named in the prompt before generating any prose
Let the tool summarize the meeting in prose and copy the bullets into the tracker herself the next morning
Ask the tool to generate a long narrative email and paste that into the tracker
Send the raw meeting transcript and let the tracker decide which words are the columns
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example shows Ali naming the exact fields (item, owner, status, blocker) in the prompt and asking for a JSON list before any prose, so every row arrives with its labels attached and the tracker reads them without relabeling. The other options all describe the prose handoff that forces the re-typing she was trying to escape.

questions.question: According to the lesson, what is the single best way to get a tool to match the shape you want?
options: Show it one complete, filled-in example and tell it to match those exact field names
Explain in technical detail how JSON keys and values are parsed
Ask for a longer response so there is more material to work with
Leave the format unspecified so the tool uses its best judgment
questions.explanation: The lesson's fourth step for defining fields says the single best way to get a tool to match a shape is to show the finished shape once and ask for the same field names, so the downstream step reads cleanly with no relabeling. The other options contradict the lesson's emphasis on an explicit, consistent example.

questions.question: A colleague asks you whether her output should be structured or free prose. Per the lesson, which single question settles it?
options: Who is doing the reading: a person who will act on it, or a spreadsheet, tracker, or automation
How many words the output should contain
Which chat tool generated the answer
Whether the answer contains any numbers at all
questions.explanation: The lesson closes by framing the whole art as one decision: decide who the consumer is. If a person will act on it, prose. If a spreadsheet, tracker, or any software will read it, structure. The other factors (length, tool, presence of numbers) are not the deciding question per the lesson.

questions.question: Nadia wants her weekly client brief to come back the same shape every Monday so her sponsor can scan it in thirty seconds. Per the lesson, what is the single most important thing to write once and keep stable?
options: The fixed frame: the role, audience, tone, output format, and review criteria that never change from week to week
The exact numbers that appeared in last week's brief
A fresh, fully rewritten prompt every Monday so each brief is unique
The name of the chat tool she happens to be using that week
questions.explanation: The lesson argues the value of a template is mostly in the fixed frame, not the fill-in. Nadia's stability comes from a frame (role, audience, tone, format, criteria) written once, so only the four slots change. The other options either vary the frame itself or treat the fresh material, not the stable frame, as the source of consistency.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the right way to keep a template's variable slot from being misread as part of the instruction?
options: Mark the variable input as its own clearly labeled slot (a named bracket or divider) so the model treats it as today's data, not a rule
Hide the fresh material entirely so the model has to guess what changed
Write the fresh input in the same tone as the instructions and let the model sort it out
Add as many slots as possible so every detail has its own placeholder
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Anthropic's guidance that structuring a prompt so the variable input is clearly marked reduces the chance the model misreads a slot as part of the instruction. Hiding the input, blending it into the instructions, and adding sprawling slots all contradict the lesson's emphasis on few, well-named slots and clearly separating the variable from the fixed.

questions.question: A colleague asks whether she should build a reusable template for an irregular, judgment-heavy task that happens once or twice a year. Per the lesson, what is the right call?
options: Do not build it; a template only pays off when the task recurs often and the frame stays stable, and a one-off leaves the setup unused
Build it anyway because every task benefits from a fixed format
Build it and force the task to fit the frame, since templates always improve output
Build a separate template for every single variation the task could hit
questions.explanation: The lesson says a template earns its keep only when two things are true: the task recurs often enough that the setup pays for itself, and the frame is genuinely stable across runs. A rare, judgment-heavy, irregular task is exactly the case the lesson flags where a one-off prompt is the better choice. The other options recommend templates where the lesson recommends against them.

questions.question: Per the lesson, what is the full cost of a workflow that people most often forget to price in?
options: The maintenance cost, the recurring effort to keep the workflow working as inputs, tools, and the task itself change
The cost of the software license for the tool that runs the workflow
The one-time build cost of writing the template and setting up the connection
The cost of training a colleague to run the workflow for you
questions.explanation: The lesson says people price a workflow by its build cost, but the full cost is build plus maintenance, and the maintenance cost is the one that sneaks up on you: the recurring effort to keep it working as inputs, tools, and the task drift.

questions.question: According to the lesson, why is an unmaintained workflow worse than a one-off?
options: Because it looks permanent and reliable, so you trust it, and your trust rises while its accuracy falls as the world around it changes
Because a one-off always produces better output than a saved workflow
Because unmaintained workflows are automatically deleted by the tool
Because a one-off requires no review at all, while a workflow always needs one
questions.explanation: The lesson argues a one-off is honest about being temporary, while an unmaintained workflow looks reliable and you trust it, which is when it hurts you: the human is the last safeguard, and stopping the check removes the only thing keeping it safe.

questions.question: Priya runs the three-question test on two tasks. Which task should she leave as a one-off, and why?
options: The quarterly executive review deck, because its shape changes every quarter, so the frame is never stable and the setup is never repaid
The weekly team status rollup, because it is low-risk and therefore not worth owning
The quarterly executive review deck, because it is high-stakes and therefore too important to automate
The weekly team status rollup, because it recurs too often to maintain
questions.explanation: The lesson's worked example shows Priya owns the weekly rollup because it is the same shape every week, and leaves the quarterly deck as a one-off because its format, audience, and content change each quarter, so the frame is never stable and the build is never repaid.

questions.question: Priya's monthly vendor summary came back wrong: the overdue-deliveries flag was empty and the tone drifted hedged. Per the lesson, what is the most reliable way for her to work out why?
options: Consult her changelog, which records each change with a date and a reason, and trace the broken behavior back to the exact edit that caused it
Rewrite the prompt from scratch so it looks fresh and hope the regenerated output improves
Regenerate the output repeatedly until it happens to come out close to what she wants
Turn the tool off and do the summary by hand from now on without examining the cause
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that a version problem is best diagnosed by evidence: a changelog with dated, reason-based entries turns a guessing game into a lookup. In Priya's case the log showed she had moved the overdue flag into a variable slot, which is why it went missing. Rewriting, regenerating blindly, or abandoning the tool all skip the diagnosis the lesson recommends.

questions.question: Per the lesson, which habit is what makes a rollback possible at all?
options: Never overwriting the version that works: save a known-good baseline and always work on a copy, so any new change can be undone by returning to it
Keeping every edit in one running file so the most recent version replaces the older one every time
Recording only the changes that turned out badly and ignoring the rest
Writing every change without a date so the sequence is shorter and easier to scan
questions.explanation: The lesson says the human translation of Semantic Versioning's 'contents must not be modified' rule is: keep the good version intact and never edit it in place, save the new attempt as a new version so the known-good baseline survives to be rolled back to. Overwriting, recording only failures, and dropping dates all contradict that and make rollback impossible or misleading.

questions.question: A colleague says versioning is a coding practice that does not apply to him because he only works in a chat tool. Based on the lesson, what is the right response?
options: Versioning applies to instructions too, since editing a prompt, toggling a setting, changing the data, or the tool updating are all version changes worth recording
Agree, because versioning can only work for code and has no use for prompts
Tell him versioning matters only when a workflow involves a spreadsheet
Tell him to version only the output the tool produces, never the inputs
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly says versioning applies to instructions, not just code: a rewritten prompt, a changed tool setting, different data pasted in, and the tool itself updating are all version changes, and are exactly what a changelog is for. The other options dismiss or misplace the habit the lesson recommends.

questions.question: Priya ran her monthly vendor summary in her tool's draft mode before sending it. Per the lesson, what made this a dry run?
options: It used her real input and produced the real output, but stopped before anything was sent, changed, or scheduled, so she saw the result with none of the consequences
It used made-up sample data so the real numbers were never touched at all
It sent the summary to a single test recipient and then to the full list
It skipped the review step entirely so the workflow ran faster
questions.explanation: The lesson defines a dry run as a run that uses your real input, produces the real output, and then stops before anything reaches the outside world, nothing is sent, changed, or scheduled. That is exactly what Priya's draft mode did. The other options describe either fake data, a partial real send, or skipping the check, none of which is a dry run.

questions.question: Priya found that one vendor row with a long, hyphenated name caused the tool to truncate the amount and make the total come up short. Per the lesson, what is this an example of?
options: An edge case, a problem that occurs only at an extreme operating parameter, like an input longer than the tool's comfortable range, rather than in its normal range
A happy path, the normal input where everything is in order
A versioning error, because the prompt had not been saved as a new version
A dry run failure, because the tool refused to produce any output
questions.explanation: The lesson defines an edge case as a problem that occurs only at an extreme operating parameter, the boundary of what a process can handle, and cites long, oddly formatted inputs as a classic example. Priya's long hyphenated vendor name is exactly that. The happy path is the normal input, so it is not this; the failure is not a versioning or dry-run issue.

questions.question: A colleague says he does not need to check his AI workflow's output because the tool has never been wrong. Based on the lesson, what is the right response?
options: Bad output is rarely obviously wrong, it is smooth and plausible, so you should dry run, probe edge cases, and read the output like a critic every time before it ships
Agree, because a tool that has never been wrong will keep being right
Tell him to check only the numbers and ignore everything else
Tell him testing matters only when a workflow sends emails, not when it drafts text
questions.explanation: The lesson argues that bad output from an AI workflow is wrong the way a confident person can be wrong, smooth and plausible, and that the discipline is to read output like a critic, not a friend, checking numbers, invented support, tone drift, and the confident empty. A history of being right is no reason to stop checking. The other options either dismiss the need or narrow it incorrectly.
